summary: Introduces the Remote Monitoring family of MIB modules, explaining how the documents in the RMON framework relate to one another. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3577 explains how the RMON monitoring modules fit together. It describes what a monitor or probe is, the five goals the family was built for, and the list of MIB modules that make up the framework, showing for each one which layer of the network it measures at and which layer it groups the results by. It also names the objects the modules share, such as the protocol directory and the control tables.

subtitle: A map of the Remote Monitoring MIB modules and the pieces they share

tldr.problem: RMON is not one MIB module but a family of related documents, and it is hard to see which of them apply to a given measurement without reading each one.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the documents, sorts them by the layer at which they take measurements and the layer at which they aggregate them, and then names the infrastructure pieces they all build on: a media-independent table, the protocol directory, the application directory, data sources, capabilities objects and control tables.
tldr.outcome: A reader can place a module in the framework before reading it, and can see which shared objects it will rely on. The document defines nothing itself and points to the other documents for the details, including their security sections.

facts.value: 10, from Ethernet statistics to the event group

facts.label: Protocol layer identifier
facts.value: 4 octets per layer of the protocol directory

today: RFC 3577 is an Informational memo published in August 2003, produced by the RMON MIB working group, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes documents rather than defining new ones, so the detail of each module, including its security considerations, stays in the module's own document.

sections.title: What RMON Is
sections.content:
Remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, are instruments that exist for the purpose of managing or monitoring a network. They are often stand-alone devices that devote significant internal resources to that purpose, and an organisation may employ many of them, up to one per network segment. They may also be used to manage a geographically remote network, such as a provider's support centre managing a client network or an enterprise's central support organisation managing a remote site.

That device-oriented definition was taken literally when the work started, and RMON devices were purpose-built probes dedicated to implementing the RMON MIB modules. Cards then appeared that added RMON capability to a hub, switch or router, and RMON also became a software capability added to network equipment and applications running on servers or clients. In each case the RMON capability serves as a dedicated network management resource for activities ranging from long-term data collection and analysis to ad-hoc firefighting.

Most of the earliest RMON capabilities were based on promiscuous capture of packets on a network segment. Over time more capabilities were added that did not depend on that, and the newest documents allow several techniques of data gathering, with promiscuous packet capture as only one of the implementation options. The framework itself sits in the Internet Standard Management Framework, where managed objects are reached through the Management Information Base (MIB) with SNMP, and the objects are defined using SMIv2.
sections.plainLanguage: A monitor, or probe, is a device whose job is to watch a network and collect information about it. It can be a dedicated box, a card in a switch, or software in a router. The document explains how that idea grew and what the family of modules has become.

sections.title: The Five Goals of RMON
sections.content:
The document sets out five goals for the framework.

  • Offline operation. A management station is sometimes not in constant contact with its remote monitoring devices, by design to lower communication costs over a wide area or dial-up link, or by accident when a network failure affects the link. RMON therefore allows a probe to be configured to perform diagnostics and collect statistics continuously, even when communication with the management station is not possible or efficient, and the probe may then try to notify the management station when an exceptional condition occurs.
  • Proactive monitoring. With the resources available on the monitor, it can continuously run diagnostics and log network performance. The monitor is always available at the onset of a failure, can notify the management station of it, and can store historical information about the failure that the management station can play back to diagnose the cause further.
  • Problem detection and reporting. The monitor can be configured to recognise conditions, most notably error conditions, and check for them continuously. When one occurs, the event may be logged and management stations may be notified in a number of ways.
  • Value added data. Because the monitor is a network resource dedicated to management and sits directly on the monitored part of the network, it can add value to what it collects, for example by highlighting the hosts that generate the most traffic or errors, which gives the management station precisely the information it needs for a class of problems.
  • Multiple managers. An organisation may have several management stations, for different units or functions and for disaster recovery, so the monitor has to deal with more than one management station, potentially using its resources concurrently.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework was built around five ideas: a probe keeps working when the link to the manager is down, it is already watching when a failure starts, it recognises and reports trouble, it can point at the hosts causing the trouble, and it can serve several managers at once.

sections.title: The RMON Documents
sections.content:
Each document in the framework defines some new behaviour and the managed objects that configure, control and monitor it. The document lists fourteen of them. RMON-1 focuses on layer 2 and provides link-layer statistics, alarms when thresholds are crossed, and the ability to filter and capture packet contents, in groups for Ethernet statistics, history control, Ethernet history, alarms, hosts, top-N hosts, conversations, filters, packet capture and events. The Token Ring Extensions add the same functions for Token Ring media. RMON-2 extends the architecture beyond the link layer to the application layer, adding a protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network layer and application layer host and matrix groups, user history and probe configuration.

The later documents extend the family in specific directions: SMON adds RMON-like functions for switched networks, IFTOPN lets a switch sort its interfaces and send only the top ones, DSMON adds counters for Differentiated Services codepoints, HCRMON adds high capacity tables and a media-independent table, the APM MIB measures application performance as the end user experiences it, the TPM MIB drills down into sub-application transactions, the SSPM MIB generates synthetic traffic to test performance, the high capacity alarm extensions add thresholding for 64-bit counters, and RAQMON extends the framework to monitor end devices such as IP phones and mobile phones.

Two criteria tell the modules apart. The first is the layer at which a MIB takes measurements: the RMON MIB measures data-link attributes such as packets, bytes and errors, while the APM MIB measures application attributes such as response time, and measuring at higher layers requires deeper analysis of the packet and, for many application measurements, stateful flow analysis. The second is the layer at which it aggregates those measurements: RMON-1 aggregates to the link, the hardware address or the hardware address pair, all data-link concepts, while RMON-2 takes the same data-link metrics and aggregates them by network address, transport protocol or application protocol. A MIB may measure at one level and aggregate at another, and a MIB may function at several levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Each module measures something and then groups the results. RMON-1 counts packets and errors at the link and groups them by address; RMON-2 counts the same things but groups them by protocol or address higher up; the application module measures how long a user waited. Two questions identify any module: what it measures and how it groups the answers.

sections.title: The Pieces the Modules Share
sections.content:
The documents are tied together by a common purpose, similar collection methods and shared infrastructure components.

  • The media independent table holds the statistics common to most media, such as counts of packets and octets, and forms a super class from which interface-specific tables are inherited, so common statistics can be monitored even for media types that are unknown.
  • The protocol directory lets the agent list the protocols it can decode, count, categorise and time, and entries can be added, deleted and configured. Each entry is identified by a protocol identifier, a hierarchically formatted octet string built up from successive protocol encapsulations, where each layer is a four-octet identifier of the child protocol within the context of its parent. A one-octet parameter field per layer records options such as the ability to count fragmented packets, and the index of the directory table is the identifier, the parameters and their length fields.
  • The application directory and the appLocalIndex identify applications and application verbs for the application and transport monitoring modules, drawn from the protocol directory, from HTTP filters or from user-defined tables.
  • A data source is a pointer to the entity data is collected from, in one of three forms: a port, a VLAN, or a physical entity in the agent.
  • Capabilities objects let an application find out which groups and functions a probe supports, without trial and error, and they are read-only indications rather than a way to configure the probe.
  • Control tables hold the parameters for a collection operation, and the results go in separate data tables. Because the parameters describe the resulting data, many can be changed only when the control entry is invalid, so the way to change them is to delete the control entry, which also reclaims the resources used by its data.

Two facilities help several managers share a probe. EntryStatus or RowStatus objects let two managers avoid creating the same control entry, and an owner string identifies who set a control entry up, so that managers can share an existing entry rather than create an identical one, identify each other to cooperate over resources, find entries they own but have forgotten after a crash, and decide when to override someone else's entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The modules are not separate projects. They all lean on the same building blocks: a table of statistics that works for any kind of link, a list of the protocols the probe understands, a way to point at what to watch, and a way to say what the probe can do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document is a description of existing documents and as such it has no security impact of its own. For the security questions raised by each part of the framework, the reader is directed to the Security Considerations sections of the respective documents.

Two other points in the document bear on how the framework is used rather than on its security. The capabilities objects are read-only, so an application learns what a probe supports without changing its configuration, and an agent should set them at initialisation and leave them alone afterwards. The control tables need the owner string and the status objects to stay usable when several managers share one probe, because the resources involved are typically the memory and computation the function needs.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds no security rules of its own, because it defines nothing new. The security questions of each RMON module are covered in that module's own document.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH MODULE MEASURES AND WHERE IT AGGREGATES

items.title: MediaIndependent table
items.text: Statistics common to most media, inherited by interface-specific tables, so unknown media can still be monitored.

items.title: Protocol directory
items.text: The inventory of protocols the agent can decode, count, categorise and time, with a four-octet identifier per protocol layer.

items.title: Application directory
items.text: Identifies applications and application verbs through the appLocalIndex, drawn from the protocol directory, HTTP filters or user-defined tables.

items.title: Data source
items.text: A pointer to where data is collected from: a port, a VLAN or a physical entity in the agent.

items.title: Capabilities
items.text: Read-only objects that list the groups a probe supports, so an application need not find out by trial and error.

items.title: Control tables
items.text: Read-write tables holding the parameters of a collection operation, with the results in separate read-only data tables.
